title: Simulated Production Sandbox — jot
content:
Quick brain-dump for a personal PRD/sketch: simulated production sandbox for Redwood API usage by engineers and non-engineer power-users. Rough idea: a local or cloud-hosted dev mode that mimics production characteristics (latency, token accounting, failures, rollouts, model variants) so teams can test integration, cost regressions, and UX edge cases without hitting prod Dedicated/Hosted endpoints.

Why: we get recurring support asks where customers see different behaviour locally vs. prod because of batching, prefix caching, or fallback routing. Also onboarding templates assume deterministic responses; when production uses dynamic fallbacks or degraded-quality models, UX breaks. Having a realistic-but-safe sandbox will reduce friction for early validation and troubleshooting and speed up product experimentation.

Primary goals (MVP):
- Reproduce production-ish latencies and variance (configurable distributions).
- Simulate token billing and quota exhaustion scenarios (soft limits, hard limits).
- Simulate routing policies: forced fallback to cheaper/quantized variants, region fallback, and canary traffic split.
- Inject controlled errors: transient timeouts, OOM-like 503s, partial response truncation.
- Offer a straightforward dev experience: single-file config + local CLI that proxies requests to Redwood SDK/HTTP with hooks.

Non-goals (MVP):
- Exact runtime kernel parity or GPU-level perf. Not intended to replace Dedicated test clusters.
- Full fidelity of streaming/chunking implementation. Streaming will be approximated for UX tests.

Personas:
- Product engineer: needs to validate rollout responses and ensure client UI handles fallbacks correctly.
- Platform/infra engineer: test error handling, quotas, and tracing integration locally.
- Solutions engineer / SE: create reproducible demos for customers that reflect expected infra behaviour.
- PM / Designer: check perceived latency and progressive loading UX before releasing.

Core flows for MVP:
1) Quick start: install CLI or dev dependency (npm / pip), run `rw-sim init` in repo -> example config generated with 3 scenarios (optimistic, typical, constrained).
2) Proxy mode: `rw-sim proxy --config sim.yml` starts an HTTP proxy that accepts Redwood API calls and returns simulated responses (supports REST + SDK interception hooks).
3) Scenario runner: ability to run a named scenario (e.g., `rw-sim run canary-fallback`) that enacts routing policies for a time window, useful in integration tests.
4) Recording/Replay: optionally record a short trace of real requests to create a replayable dataset that can later be used to simulate exact sequence of events.

User stories (rough):
- As an engineer, I want local dev to occasionally route to a quantized variant so I can validate degradation handling. Acceptance: a toggle causes ~10% of requests to be returned from a cheaper model response file with changed token cost metadata.
- As a PM, I want to compare perceived latency between two scenarios. Acceptance: CLI produces p50/p95 measures over N runs and a small timeline snapshot.
- As an SE, I want to reproduce a customer timeout that happened in prod. Acceptance: import trace and replay with injected 503 at the same request index.
- As an infra engineer, I want to simulate token quota hitting mid-session to ensure cookie/session UX remains consistent. Acceptance: session-level quota exhaustion can be triggered after X tokens and returns the same error shape as prod.

API / UX sketches:
- sim.yml example:
  name: "canary-fallback"
  latency: {mean_ms: 120, jitter_ms: 50}   # random draw logic
  routing:
    - variant: redwood-2.1-quant
      weight: 0.1
    - variant: redwood-2.1
      weight: 0.9
  failures:
    - at_request: 35
      type: timeout
      frequency: once
  token_quota: {limit: 10000, trigger_after: 3000, behavior: hard}

- CLI commands:
  rw-sim init
  rw-sim proxy --config sim.yml --port 3001
  rw-sim run --scenario canary-fallback --duration 15m
  rw-sim record --target https://api.redwood.ai --out sample.trace

Instrumentation & fidelity notes:
- For token billing simulation, reuse Redwood tokenization logic in the dev package so token counts match SDK behaviour.
- Latency simulation: use pluggable distributions (constant, gaussian, heavy-tail) and optional per-request sequence profiles (to simulate bursty traffic).
- Response substitution: for fallback models, either (a) stash canned response files per prompt pattern, or (b) run a lightweight on-device open model if available (opt-in) for better fidelity.
- For streaming: break response into chunks with delays to simulate partial streaming; support SSE/Fetch streams depending on SDK.

Metrics & validation:
- Output a lightweight summary including p50/p95 latency, token counts, number of simulated fallbacks, and error rates.
- Unit/integration tests should assert that scenarios are reproducible (given fixed random seed).

Privacy & safety:
- By default, local recording should redact PII and provide an opt-in flag to record raw content for debugging.
- If using any cloud-hosted replay service, ensure KMS + access control and a TTL for replay traces.

Backward-compatibility / impact on existing SDKs:
- Provide SDK interception via environment variable (e.g., REDWOOD_SIM_PROXY) so no SDK change required for basic proxying.
- Longer-term: lightweight dev dependency that can be imported for more advanced programmatic scenarios.

Possible implementation approaches (tradeoffs):
- Pure proxy-based: simplest; intercept live requests and manipulate responses on-the-fly. Pros: fastest to ship. Cons: depends on stable prod shapes.
- Replay engine: record traces and replay deterministically. Pros: reproducible; useful for SEs. Cons: needs storage and sanitization.
- Embedded fake runtime: ship small deterministic response generator for common prompts. Pros: highest fidelity for certain flows. Cons: maintenance overhead.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Should we allow seeding with real model outputs (for > fidelity) or only generated canned responses? (privacy + IP).
- How much parity do we need for streaming semantics? Minimal MVP vs. nice-to-have.
- Where does this live in product org: devexp repo vs. SDK repo? (ownership + release cadence).
- Do we lean into a quick web UI for scenario authoring or start CLI-only?

Rough roadmap (personal sketch):
- Week 0-2: prototype proxy with latency + simple routing (local only).
- Week 2-5: add token accounting + quota injection + simple recording.
- Week 5-8: support streaming chunking + canned response substitution + basic CLI UX polish.
- Week 8-12: documentation, examples for common product flows (canary, cost-regression test, quota exhaustion), outreach with a couple internal SEs for feedback.

Next steps (for me):
- Sketch a minimal sim.yml schema and wire up a tiny Node/Python proxy that adds latency and toggles a fallback.
- Loop in Imogen (obs/devexp) for telemetry needs and Luca for tokenization parity.
- Create a simple demo repo that uses the SDK against the proxy and shows a UI handling a fallback.

Notes to self: keep config intentionally opinionated (not 100% flexible) — MVP should answer 3-4 core problems well. Focus on friction reduction: `rw-sim init` + one command to start proxy + one example test that asserts fallback handling.

Random ideas (parking lot):
- Cloud-hosted shareable scenario links for SE demos (with TTL).
- Marketplace of canned scenarios curated by Solutions/Support for common customer issues.
- A "stress test" mode that simulates heavy multi-tenant burst patterns to validate autoscaling logic (could be useful for Dedicated teams).

End of jot. Will iterate and turn into a short PRD if PM buy-in looks positive.
